stories.title: In Long Island Real Estate in 2027, Tight Supply Will Be a Key Driver
stories.excerpt: As 2027 approaches, real estate development on Long Island presents a mix of challenges and opportunities. Interest rates moved higher in 2026, and tighter lending standards have placed additional pressure on project financing. We expect financing costs to stay at or above current levels through 2027. Yet, Long island’s underlying market fundamentals remain strong, particularly in sectors where demand continues to outpace supply. Limited housing inventory and opportunities to reposition well-located aging commercial properties will continue to support investment across the region. Capital has not disappeared. Long Island investment sales reached $1.8 billion in the first half of 2026, up 21.2 percent year-over-year, according to Cushman & Wakefield. But lenders and investors will remain selective, favoring disciplined underwriting and experienced developers who understand the local market. Project selection will be critical as developers balance long-term demand against current financing costs. Scott Burman. Photo: Courtesy Burman. Housing is where we expect the most activity in 2027. Multifamily demand remains strong, supported by limited inventory, affordability challenges, and Long Island’s rapidly growing population of adults age 65 and older, underscoring the need for a broader range of housing options. Policy is beginning to help as well. 2027 will also mark the first full year under New York’s 2026 SEQRA reforms, which are designed to streamline environmental review for qualifying housing developments without overriding local zoning and permitting requirements. Another major opportunity is repositioning. According to Schuckman Realty, Long Island retail vacancy was 4.2 percent in mid-2026, asking rents were up about 9 percent year-over-year, and virtually no new retail space was being built. In a market this tight, the opportunity lies in transforming aging and underutilized commercial properties, particularly traditional shopping malls, into destinations
bullets: Long Island housing supply remains tight; demand outpaces inventory through 2027
NY SEQRA 2026 reforms streamline environmental review for qualifying housing projects
Financing costs expected to stay elevated through 2027; multifamily remains primary activity
stories.summary: Long Island's multifamily market is supported by limited housing inventory, strong affordability pressure, and growing 65+ population through 2027. Interest rates and tighter lending standards persist, keeping financing costs elevated. New York's 2026 SEQRA reforms streamline environmental review for housing developments, reducing approval timelines and regulatory friction for qualifying projects.
stories.impact: SEQRA reforms lower entitlement risk and timeline for Long Island/Queens projects, creating a window to fast-track acquisitions and development approvals before market tightens further. Tight supply + policy tailwinds = strong risk-adjusted returns for projects shovel-ready by 2027.

stories.title: Mamdani Scores Critical Court Victory for Rent Freeze
stories.excerpt: Just ahead of the Thanksgiving weekend, a Manhattan Supreme Court judge sided with New York Mayor Zohran Mamdani on his controversial rent freeze in a case that landlords brought against the New York City Rent Guidelines Board (RGB). The mayor called the decision “a victory for tenants, for affordability and for the principle that working New Yorkers deserve a city they can afford to live in.” The case stems from a 7-1 vote by the mayor-appointed RGB on June 26 halting rent increases for the city’s approximately 1 million rent-stabilized apartments. The judge in today’s ruling, Brendan T. Lantry, emphasized that his decision was not a vote for or against the wisdom of the RGB’s ruling, and that it “may cause negative collateral consequences,” but that the rent freeze was nevertheless legal. In a lawsuit filed in July, landlords had contended that the RGB ignored evidence of the rising expenses that rent-stabilized owners face in maintaining and upgrading their buildings. In some cases, the landlords said, the RGB ignored its own data, which “clearly signaled a rent increase,” according to Ann Korchak, board president of Small Property Owners of New York, whose members were plaintiffs in the lawsuit. “This ruling is terribly disappointing to small property owners,” Korchak said in a statement on Wednesday. “The rent freeze will push more small rent-stabilized property owners to the edge of the cliff. It denies the resources they need to maintain and operate their rent-stabilized buildings. Property taxes, water and sewer rates, and insurance, energy, heating, repair and other costs and expenses aren’t frozen. Rents should not be frozen, either.” Randy Mastro, a lawyer for the landlords in the case, said in a statement to Commercial Observer that they were “disappointed by the court’s ruling.” “The judge acknowledged multiple irregularities in the RGB’s process and, in particular, called out Mayor Mamdani’s ‘comments, promises and guarant
bullets: NYC rent freeze upheld by Manhattan court; covers ~1M rent-stabilized apartments
Mayor Mamdani's RGB vote frozen rent increases citywide as of June 26
Court ruled freeze legal despite landlord claims of rising maintenance costs
stories.summary: A Manhattan Supreme Court judge upheld NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani's controversial rent freeze imposed by the Rent Guidelines Board on June 26, affecting approximately 1 million rent-stabilized units. Landlords had sued, arguing the RGB ignored rising operational expenses, but the court found the freeze legally sound despite potential "negative collateral consequences."
stories.impact: Rent-stabilized portfolio returns compressed in NYC; reduces acquisition appeal for stabilized buildings. Underwriting for RS assets must assume zero rent growth through regulatory cycle, pressuring cap rates and valuations. Developers should focus on market-rate and new-construction projects to avoid RS exposure; policy uncertainty may also chill institutional capital for NYC multifamily conversions.

stories.title: Netflix Acquiring Historic Radford Studio Center for $380M
stories.excerpt: Netflix has reached an agreement to acquire the historic Radford Studio Center in Studio City for a reported $380 million, marking the streaming giant’s first purchase of a Los Angeles-area studio lot. The property is located at 4024 Radford Avenue, just off Ventura Blvd in the southeastern San Fernando Valley, close to Hollywood, Burbank and many other entertainment-related businesses. As reported by the L.A. Times and other sources, Goldman Sachs took control of the property in January after its previous owner, Hackman Capital Partners, defaulted on a $1.1 billion mortgage amid a slowdown in Hollywood production. Hackman and Square Mile Capital Management acquired the property for $1.85 billion in 2021. The 1.14 million-square-foot production campus features 22 soundstages, 18 office buildings and 20 bungalows. Founded in 1928 by filmmaker Mack Sennett, the studio has been home to numerous iconic television series, including Seinfeld, Gilligan’s Island, Will & Grace and The Mary Tyler Moore Show. The acquisition represents a significant expansion of Netflix’s Southern California real estate holdings. The company currently leases approximately 2 million square feet of office and soundstage space in Los Angeles. Netflix intends to retain Radford’s existing studio team and maintain operations at the production campus. bullets: Netflix acquires Radford Studio Center for $380M in Studio City, LA; 1.14M sq ft
Goldman Sachs seized property after Hackman Capital defaulted on $1.1B mortgage in Jan

stories.summary: Netflix purchased the historic Radford Studio Center in Studio City for $380 million, marking its first acquisition of a Los Angeles studio lot. The 1.14 million-square-foot production campus (22 soundstages, 18 offices, 20 bungalows) was seized by Goldman Sachs in January after Hackman Capital Partners defaulted on a $1.1 billion mortgage amid Hollywood production slowdown.
stories.impact: Limited relevance to multifamily development. However, signals distress in specialized real estate financing (Hackman's $1.85B 2021 purchase now worth ~$380M) and underscores production industry consolidation. Streamer in-sourcing of studio space may reduce demand for independent soundstage leasing in LA, affecting mixed-use/studio conversion opportunities for developers.

stories.title: Fairstead Closes $17M Affordable Housing Transaction in Oklahoma
stories.excerpt: Fairstead announced its $16.5 million acquisition of London Square Village Apartments, a 200-unit project-based Section 8 community in Oklahoma City, Oklahoma, and plans for a comprehensive rehabilitation of the property. The transaction marks Fairstead’s first acquisition in Oklahoma. London Square Village Apartments consists of 200 units across 18 two-story residential buildings and a community center. The community includes 24 one-bedroom, 96 two-bedroom and 80 three-bedroom homes, with all units reserved for households earning at or below 60% of the area median income.  “Expanding into Oklahoma represents an important step in Fairstead’s mission to preserve sustainable, reliable affordable housing for communities across the country,” said Jeff Goldberg, Founder and CEO of Fairstead. The acquisition will preserve London Square Village Apartments as affordable housing through 4% federal LIHTC equity from R4 Capital and tax-exempt bond financing issued by the Oklahoma Housing Finance Agency, with R4 Capital also serving as lender. Join us for the Connect Midwest Multifamily conference on the afternoon of Tuesday, June 8, 2027, at Joe’s Live in Rosemont, Illinois. stories.summary: Fairstead closed its first Oklahoma acquisition: London Square Village Apartments, a 200-unit Section 8 community in Oklahoma City for $16.5 million. All units are reserved for households earning at or below 60% of area median income. Financing sources include 4% federal LIHTC equity from R4 Capital and tax-exempt bonds issued by the Oklahoma Housing Finance Agency.
stories.impact: Signals institutional capital expanding into Tier-2 affordable housing markets. Oklahoma City's affordable housing pipeline strengthens; developer should monitor other LIHTC/Section 8 recycling opportunities in OK for acquisition or new development. Preservation/rehab model is lower-risk than ground-up development in secondary markets.

stories.title: Dwight Capital Finances $52M Loan for Mixed-Use Multifamily Community in Michigan
stories.excerpt: Dwight Capital has closed a $52 million HUD 223(f) loan for Griffin Royal Oak, a 245-unit luxury mixed-use multifamily community in the heart of Royal Oak, Michigan. Developed by Singh Development, the property features a five-story residential building, an attached parking garage, and four ground-floor commercial spaces totaling 9,000 square feet. Strategically located near downtown Royal Oak, Griffin Royal Oak is surrounded by pedestrian-friendly sidewalks, boutiques, salons, and retail shops, and more than 70 restaurants. The property’s luxury residences, ground-floor retail, and walkable location reflect Singh Development’s focus on thoughtfully designed communities in desirable locations. “Griffin Royal Oak represents the type of community we have focused on developing for more than five decades—high-quality residential environments in strong, established markets,” said Saab Grewal of Singh Development. Dwight Capital’s Karnveer Bal and Alex Shoenfeld originated the loan on behalf of Singh Development, an established, family-owned real estate development and investment company. Join us for the Connect Midwest Multifamily conference on the afternoon of Tuesday, June 8, 2027, at Joe’s Live in Rosemont, Illinois. Royal Oak's downtown walkability + retail/restaurant density attract quality institutional capital; developers should prioritize similar infill mixed-use sites in Detroit MSA submarkets for lower refinance risk.

stories.title: Host Hotels Rounds Out $202M Brooklyn Hotel Buy With $29M Retail, Parking Acquisition
stories.excerpt: Host Hotels & Resorts has secured three retail spaces and an indoor parking area at its newly acquired hotel asset in Brooklyn’s Dumbo neighborhood. The Bethesda, Md.-based real estate investment trust, through the entity Brooklyn Bridge Hotel Owner, acquired the commercial condo units and parking space at 90 Furman Street from a Starwood Capital Group entity, according to property records filed Wednesday. All four properties were built in 2015, according to city tax records, and adjoin Host Hotel’s newest portfolio addition, 1 Hotel Brooklyn Bridge at 60 Furman Street. Host Hotel acquired the hotel’s 85-year leasehold interest from Starwood in a $202 million all-cash deal announced earlier this month. The 195-key hotel marks a significant feather in Host Hotel’s cap, as the operator expects 1 Hotel Brooklyn Bridge to be among its top 10 assets based on full-year estimates. A second agreement, this one concerning the takeover and restructuring of an existing $113 million debt on the properties at 90 Furman and 60 Furman Street, was also filed in city records Wednesday. The properties’ existing mortgage was previously held by Sumitomo Mitsui Banking, according to the filing, and has now been assigned to the entity TRS NY Lender. The same entity has previously been linked by The Real Deal to the New York State Teachers’ Retirement System of NYC, which financed Host Hotels’ 2024 purchase of Starwood’s 1 Hotel Central Park at 1414 Avenue of the Americas. That $265 million deal was in one of that year’s top 10 investment sales. Host Hotels’ recent acquisition of the Dumbo hotel came on the heels of a $127 million all-cash purchase of the 308-room Renaissance Dallas at Plano Legacy West Hotel in Texas. The seller was a joint venture of Paceline Equity Partners and Aravest. Spokespeople for Host Hotels and Starwood did not respond to requests for comment. Emily Davis can be reached at edavis@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: Host Hotels acquires three retail units + parking at 90 Furman Street, Brooklyn for $29M

stories.summary: Host Hotels & Resorts acquired three retail spaces and an indoor parking facility at 90 Furman Street in Brooklyn's DUMBO neighborhood for $29 million, adjoining its $202 million acquisition of the 195-key 1 Hotel Brooklyn Bridge at 60 Furman Street. The hotel lease (85-year term) is expected to generate top-10 portfolio performance for Host.
stories.impact: Limited direct multifamily impact. However, signals strong capital flows to Brooklyn waterfront hospitality; retail and mixed-use conversion opportunities adjacent to successful hotel assets may face increased competition for land/space. DUMBO's hospitality strength may suppress residential conversion economics vs. hotel/retail hold.

stories.title: Thor Equities Buys San Francisco Office/Retail Asset for $50.5M, Lands $51.8M Loan
stories.excerpt: Thor Equities has acquired 55 Stockton Street, a boutique Class A office and retail property in San Francisco’s Union Square district, from Zaber Corporation for $50.5 million. The company also secured $51.8 million in acquisition financing from Prime Finance. Also known as the National Center Building, the eight-story, 136,714-square-foot property is situated at the corner of Stockton and O’Farrell streets, one block south of Union Square. Built in 1988 and renovated in 2023, the building features three floors of retail space with boutique office space above. Office tenants include Chalk AI, Harness and Taylor & Associates Architects. The acquisition expands Thor’s presence in the Union Square district. The firm acquired nearby 146 Geary St., home to Bang & Olufsen’s flagship store, for $20.5 million in August. Thor also owns 152 Geary St., occupied by Banana Republic. The property offers convenient access to public transportation and is surrounded by prominent retail, dining and hospitality destinations. Newmark’s Chris Kramer, Ricky Braha, Tim Polglase and Dante DiStefano arranged the financing on behalf of Thor Equities. The 1988 building (2023 renovation) features three retail floors and boutique office space and is Thor's latest Union Square expansion.

stories.title: OC Investor Group Buys Two Apartment Properties in Venice
stories.excerpt: A group of private Orange County-based investors acquired two multifamily properties totaling 40 units in the coastal Los Angeles community of Venice for $14.23 million. The properties, located at 1400 and 1500 Venice Blvd., were sold by Advanced Real Estate Group. The transaction, which partly included 1031 exchange capital, worked out to $355,662 per unit and $430 per square foot. Colliers’ Kitty Wallace represented the seller and, along with colleague Andy Eberhard, also represented the buyers. Built in 1988 and 1985, respectively, the properties encompass 33,072 square feet of building area and offer 77 parking spaces. Neither property is subject to the City of Los Angeles Rent Stabilization Ordinance. The 31-unit property at 1400 Venice Blvd. features renovated interiors, a fitness center, a rooftop lounge and subterranean parking. The nine-unit property at 1500 Venice Blvd. sold above its asking price for approximately $3.43 million, representing a 5.13% capitalization rate. The new ownership plans to continue the previous ownership’s unit renovation program. stories.summary: A private Orange County investor group acquired two multifamily properties totaling 40 units in Venice, Los Angeles for $14.23 million ($355,662 per unit). The properties—built in 1988 and 1985—are not subject to LA's Rent Stabilization Ordinance. The 31-unit property features renovated interiors and amenities; the smaller 9-unit asset sold above ask at a 5.13% cap rate.
stories.impact: Venice market-rate supply remains tight despite rental compression elsewhere in LA. Non-RSO properties command premium valuations; developers should prioritize Venice ground-up development or acquisition in adjacent Westside submarkets (Palms, Mar Vista) where RSO pressure is lower and rent growth more sustainable.

stories.title: Flight to Quality Deepens Divide Among Major U.S. Office Markets
stories.excerpt: The U.S. office market is showing more signs of improvement, but the recovery remains uneven across the nation’s biggest cities. The national office vacancy rate declined 140 basis points annually to 17.2 percent in October, while average asking rents increased 1.5 percent to $33.30 per square foot, according to a report using Yardi data. Office sales totaled nearly $56.9 billion across 2,576 transactions through the first 10 months of 2026, with properties trading at an average of $197 per square foot. But the flight to quality is widening the performance gap between newer and older properties, the report found. Asking rents for Class A office space increased 2.5 percent over the past year, while rents for Class B space declined 0.3 percent. “Office employment growth doesn’t always translate into an office market rebound, and we are seeing significant market discrepancies,” Peter Kolaczynski, director of Yardi Research, said in the report. “One consistency, though, is that outdated and less amenitized buildings are facing the most pressure, while new deliveries are offering best-in-class product and obtaining rent premiums.” Manhattan led the nation’s largest office markets in investment volume, construction activity, asking rents and occupancy in October. Investors traded more than $6.2 billion worth of Manhattan office properties in the first 10 months of the year at an average of $533 per square foot. Meanwhile, Manhattan’s average asking rents increased 9.5 percent annually to $74.44 per square foot, more than double the national average. The borough also had 3.73 million square feet of office space under construction, the largest development pipeline in the country. Miami recorded the strongest annual office rent growth among the markets tracked, with asking rates jumping 12.8 percent to $63.58 per square foot. stories.impact: Flight to quality accelerates office-to-multifamily conversion economics: Class B/C office assets in secondary office markets face obsolescence risk, making conversion to apartments more economically viable. Developers should target Class B/C office inventory in supply-constrained multifamily metros (Austin, Denver, Raleigh, Miami) for conversion; older buildings in declining office markets offer lowest land-basis entry points.

stories.title: RXR Supplies $140M Construction Loan for Miami Rental Development
stories.excerpt: RXR has funneled $140 million into the construction of a Live Local Act rental tower near the Aventura Mall in Miami-Dade County. Group P6 is developing the 363-unit Spoke Aventura at 2600 Northeast 203rd Street. The 21-story development will rise a block west from Biscayne Boulevard, about a mile north of the 2.8 million-square-foot indoor mall and the city’s Brightline station. Construction is expected to be completed in 2028, with Moss serving as a general contractor. Morris Betesh and Ronnie Levine of Arrow Real Estate Advisors brokered the loan. More than 40 percent of units will be priced at 120 percent of the area’s median income, in accordance with Florida’s Live Local Act, which provides tax breaks and speedy approvals for developers. Amenities will include a pool deck, a fitness center, a resident lounge, coworking space and a padel court, along with ground-floor retail and a 435-space parking garage. The Boca Raton-based development firm, led by Ignacio Diaz and Jose J. Padua, paid $16 million for the 1.3-acre site in 2024. “Spoke Aventura and Group P6 represent the high-quality, well-located multifamily projects and the high-quality sponsorship that RXR’s Capital Solutions strategy is pursuing,” Russ Young, RXR’s head of investments, said in a statement. RXR, led by Scott Rechler, is a major New York investor and developer, best known for owning trophy office buildings and large-scale redevelopment, including 1211 Avenue of the Americas and the Helmsley Building. Its lending in South Florida has remained limited to a few projects, including providing a mezzanine loan to another Live Local Act project last year. Julia Echikson can be reached at jechikson@commercialobserver.com.
bullets: RXR provides $140M construction loan for Spoke Aventura, 363-unit rental in Miami-Dade

stories.summary: RXR supplied $140 million in construction financing for Spoke Aventura, a 363-unit rental tower in Miami-Dade County developed by Group P6. The 21-story property, expected to complete in 2028, is located near Aventura Mall and Brightline station. More than 40% of units qualify under Florida's Live Local Act, providing tax incentives and expedited approvals for workforce housing.
stories.impact: Florida Live Local Act financing is now competitive for Tier-1 lenders (RXR); Act's tax incentives + fast-track approvals are shifting Miami-Dade development economics favorably toward mixed-income/workforce projects near transit. Developers should layer Live Local Act incentives into Miami/Tampa/Jacksonville pro formas to improve returns on 100%+ AMI projects and compete for institutional debt.
